newsitem.title: USA: U.S. seeks Canada's help to extradite Pol Pot.
newsitem.headline: U.S. seeks Canada's help to extradite Pol Pot.

text.p: The United States has asked Canada to help extradite Khmer Rouge guerrilla chief Pol Pot from Cambodia so he can be tried by an international tribunal for crimes against humanity, U.S. officials said on Monday.

At a summit of the eight major industrialised nations in Denver last weekend, Secretary of State Madeleine Albright asked Canadian Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy to request the extradition under Canada's law against genocide.
Only Canada and Denmark have laws permitting them to make such a request, officials said. But U.S. officials told Reuters the issue was complicated and they did not have a final answer from Canada.

The United States is awaiting confirmation that Pol Pot is in custody. Although Cambodian government leaders announced he was being held by his former Khmer Rouge allies, acting State Department spokesman John Dinger said: "There have been many conflicting reports over the last week or so. Not to dismiss the latest reports, which may well be true, I can't rule out that he is in custody, and I can't rule it in."
He refused to discuss the nature of discussions on Pol Pot between the United States, Cambodia and other nations.

But Dinger stressed that "if he is in custody, if we are requested to provide any assistance, we'll certainly be willing to help in any way we can the Cambodian people to deal with this terrible history."

More than one million people were executed as enemies of Pol Pot's utopian revolution or died of disease, starvation or overwork during the Khmer Rouge's brutal 1975-79 rule. If Canada agrees to seek his extradition, the United States is ready to coordinate sending a military team to Cambodia to remove Pol Pot from the country, U.S. officials said.
One official termed it a "parallel operation in terms of logistical assistance for the Cambodians so that Pol Pot can be safely and quickly brought to a holding location."

Albright had planned to visit Cambodia this week until recent violence broke out between allies of the country's two rival co-prime ministers. Officials still hope she can make the visit but a final decision has not been made.
"The secretary has not cancelled her visit," Dinger said.

"There are two main considerations. One is the strong desire by the United States, and certainly by Secretary Albright, to demonstrate our commitment and support for the Cambodian people and their efforts to continue to develop democratic institutions...and the other one, of course, are security considerations. We have to balance the two," he said.
Albright is due to leave on Tuesday for San Francisco, then visit Vietnam and attend celebrations relating to Hong Kong's transfer to Chinese control on July 1.

Under a plan being worked out, U.S. officials said, Pol Pot would be extradited to Canada as a temporary measure until an international tribunal could be convened to try him under the international Genocide Convention. They said the aim was not to wait for a tribunal to be created before taking Pol Pot into custody.

"If this guy becomes available the Cambodian parties want to make sure his capture doesn't make things worse in Cambodia (where violence and political tensions have been on the upswing) so the first thing is to find a place to hold him," one official said.
The Cambodian government has been adamant that Pol Pot be taken out of the country for fear of mob violence and the political repercussions of his arrest.

The second problem "is what body does the prosecuting," an official said, adding: "There are a number of options that we are pursuing but we do believe that a body ought to be found that has international standing to bring him to light and prosecute the heinous war crimes."

Cambodia's first prime minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh said on Monday that Pol Pot was alive and a senior military officer said he was being held in the jungle village headquarters of a breakaway Khmer Rouge faction and would be transferred to Phnom Penh.
